standard_prerequisites.name: Fourier-space density decay
standard_prerequisites.statement: The Fourier transform of the density obeys a bound with a weight that grows in the frequency and in the product of frequency and time, with the exponent $\sigma_1$1 fixed by the hypotheses.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the estimate that the counted proof transfers to physical space.

standard_prerequisites.name: Hausdorff-Young inequality
standard_prerequisites.statement: The Lp norm of a function is controlled by the Lp' norm of its Fourier transform, with 1/p + 1/p' = 1.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the first step of the proof.

standard_prerequisites.name: Weighted derivative norms
standard_prerequisites.statement: The norm with the weight |$\nabla$x, t$\nabla$x|^n measures derivatives in space and in the time direction simultaneously.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the norm appearing in the conclusion and inside the integral.

core_obligations: Apply the Hausdorff-Young inequality to express the weighted Lp norm of the density through an integral over frequencies of the p'-th power of the Fourier transform of the density, weighted by the p' multiple of the weight (source lines 393-397).

Insert the Fourier-space decay estimate, so that the integrand becomes an explicit negative power of the weight and the integral converges exactly under the stated restriction n < $\sigma_1$1 - d(1-1/p) (source line 398).
Read off the resulting bound with the stated power of time (source line 398).

proof_roadmap.step: Hausdorff-Young converts the weighted Lp norm into a frequency integral with the dual exponent.
Feed the decay estimate into the integral and identify the convergence condition with the stated restriction on n.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the unlabelled corollary at source lines 376-391, headed [Physical-space decay]: under the hypotheses of the main theorem, for every n below $\sigma_1$1 minus d times one minus one over p, the weighted Lp norm of the density is bounded by a constant times a negative power of time. The author gave it no label, so its position in the article is part of its identity. The proof (source lines 392-399) is short but not formal: the Hausdorff-Young inequality has to be applied to the weighted norm rather than to the plain one, which is what produces the dual exponent p' inside the frequency integral, and the convergence of that integral, after the decay estimate is substituted, is exactly where the restriction on n comes from. Both the dual exponent bookkeeping and the convergence condition are absent from the statement.
